rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects carrying the widely transmitted accusative reading on a weak, nonstandard syntactic analysis; if this construction were valid, Sibawayh would have treated its parallels.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز أن تحمل القراءة المستفيضة على وجه ضعيف ليس بحد الكلام ولا وجهه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats the accusative as coordinated with an omitted purpose: God destroys some, saves others, and warns disputants about their lack of escape.
rows.anchor: أو إن يشأ يجمع بين ثلاثة أمور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author finds the proposed purpose of vengeance unsuitable after destruction is made conditional on God's will; the other cited purpose clauses may have omitted verbs before them.
rows.anchor: ويبعد تقديره لينتقم منها، لأنه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: For the jussive reading of yaʿlam, al-Zamakhshari understands three outcomes together: destruction, salvation, and warning the disputants through their having no refuge.
rows.anchor: أو إن يشأ يجمع بين ثلاثة أمور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about having no escape is governed by yaʿlam, which is suspended from taking a direct object because it introduces an embedded question.
rows.anchor: وما لهم من محيص في موضع نصب، لأن يعلم معلقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says Ibn ʿAtiyya's explanation of the Kufian label waw al-sarf actually describes the Basran account, in which an implicit masdar is coordinated with a noun.
rows.anchor: وليس قوله تعليلا لقولهم واو الصرف، إنما هو تقرير لمذهب البصريين

rows.speaker: الكوفيون
rows.claim: The Kufians hold that waw al-sarf itself governs the subjunctive, without an omitted an after it.
rows.anchor: وأما الكوفيون فإن واو الصرف ناصبة بنفسها، لا بإضمار أن بعدها

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayd calls the construction sarf, a shift from one direction to another that changes the inflection; he compares it with 3:142.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيد على الصرف كالذي في آل عمران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Coordination alone need not imply simultaneous occurrence, but waw al-sarf plus the subjunctive can express joint occurrence; the community agrees on the subjunctive in 3:142 for both strivers and patient people.
rows.anchor: ولذلك أجمع على النصب في قوله

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAli reports that Abu Bakr gave all his wealth to God's cause, prompting rebuke from Muslims and blame from disbelievers, after which this verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: عن علي، رضي الله عنه، اجتمع لأبي بكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent addressees are people generally, though another view identifies the polytheists; what is given refers to worldly goods and abundance, which are only temporary enjoyment.
rows.anchor: وما شرطية مفعول ثان لأوتيتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What God has prepared as reward for His friends is better and more lasting than worldly gifts because it does not end.
rows.anchor: وما عند الله: أي من ثوابه وما أعد لأوليائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author links the discussion of major sins to 4:31; most recite the plural kabāʾir here and in 53:32, while Hamza and al-Kisaʾi use the singular.
rows.anchor: كبائر جمعا هنا، وفي النجم، وحمزة، والكسائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects Abu al-Baqaʾ's parsing of alladhīna yajtنبūn without a conjunction because the text has a waw; he also rejects making the conditional clause a response without fa except in poetry.
rows.anchor: لأن الجملة لو كانت جواب إذا لكانت بالفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A possible parsing makes hum the subject of an omitted verb explained by yaghfirūn; the author notes a similar analysis under Sibawayh for a jussive conditional, though al-Kisaʾi and al-Farraʾ reject it.
rows.anchor: ولا يبعد جواز ذلك على مذهب سيبويه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the emphatic hum presents them as especially able to forgive: anger does not overwhelm their judgment as it does ordinary people.
rows.anchor: أي هم الأخصاء بالغفران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the fronted subject encourages people to restrain anger.
rows.anchor: وفيه حض على كسر الغضب

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A hadith repeatedly advises a questioner who asks for counsel not to become angry.
rows.anchor: أوصني، قال: لا تغضب، قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says the verse was revealed about the Ansar, whom God called to faith and obedience and who responded; before Islam they consulted together whenever an issue arose.
rows.anchor: قيل: نزلت في الأنصار، دعاهم الله

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says a people who consult one another are guided to their soundest course.
rows.anchor: ما تشاور قوم إلا هدوا لأرشد أمرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Consultation brings agreement, affection, and mutual support for good; the Prophet and later Companions consulted on war interests and legal questions.
rows.anchor: وفي الشورى اجتماع الكلمة والتحاب والتعاضد على الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shūrā is a verbal noun like fatwā meaning consultation, with an omitted noun: their affair is consultation among them.
rows.anchor: والشورى مصدر كالفتيا بمعنى التشاور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Retaliation means limiting oneself to the bounds God set and avoiding transgression.
rows.anchor: أن يقتصر على ما حده الله له ولا يعتدي

rows.speaker: النخعي
rows.claim: Al-Nakhaʿi says they disliked humiliating themselves lest the wicked become emboldened; vindication without excess is obedience and praiseworthy.
rows.anchor: كانوا يكرهون أن يذلوا أنفسهم

rows.speaker: مقاتل وهشام عن عروة
rows.claim: Muqatil and Hisham, transmitting from ʿUrwa, say the verse concerns an injured person taking retaliation from the assailant.
rows.anchor: مقاتل، وهشام عن عروة: الآية في المجروح ينتصف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says the polytheists attacked the Prophet and his Companions and expelled them from Mecca, so God permitted them to travel and aided them against their aggressors.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: تعدى المشركون على رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الكيا الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Kiya al-Tabari reads vindication as preferable against a persistent aggressor, while forgiveness is preferable when the offender repents; the following verses permit retaliation and praise patient forgiveness.
rows.anchor: الكيا الطبري: ظاهره أن الانتصار في هذا الموضع أفضل

rows.speaker: ابن بحر
rows.claim: Ibn Bahr interprets the wording as mutual support that removes the aggressor from their midst.
rows.anchor: ابن بحر: المعنى تناصروا عليه فأزالوه عنهم

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن العربي
rows.claim: Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi agrees with al-Kiya's distinction between persistent aggression and a repentant offender.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر بن العربي نحوا من قول الكيا

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most jurists say a Muslim who is wronged by another Muslim may not retaliate personally but must refer the case to the ruler or deputy; another group permits personal retaliation.
rows.anchor: الجمهور: إذا بغى مؤمن على مؤمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Equivalent recompense explains vindication and bars exceeding the injury; the unrestricted wording is qualified by evidence and by juristic analogy in many cases.
rows.anchor: هذا بيان للانتصار، أي لا يتعدى فيما

rows.speaker: ابن أبي نجيح والسدي
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Najih and al-Suddi say a person may return an insult in kind without excess; retaliation is called an evil by comparison or because it pains the offender as the initial harm did.
rows.anchor: ابن أبي نجيح، والسدي: إذا شتم، فله أن

rows.speaker: مجاهد والسدي
rows.claim: Mujahid and al-Suddi give examples: answer May God disgrace you with the same, and impose the prescribed penalty for slander that warrants the ḥadd.
rows.anchor: مجاهد، والسدي: إذا قال له أخزاك الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pardoning reconciles the offender with the victim, and God's unspecified promise of reward is immeasurably great; forgiving an offender is especially fitting because God loves no wrongdoer.
rows.anchor: فمن عفا وأصلح: أي بينه وبين خصمه بالعفو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's rejection of wrongdoing also warns victims that anger or wartime zeal can make them exceed the bounds while retaliating without noticing.
rows.anchor: من تجاوز واعتدى من المجني عليهم، إذا انتصروا

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A hadith says that on Judgment Day those who forgave people who wronged them will be summoned as people owed a reward by God and admitted to Paradise.
rows.anchor: إذا كان يوم القيامة نادى مناد من كان له أجر على الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in the promise for one who vindicates himself emphasizes the statement and can carry an oath sense; the conditional construction shifts from the literal form of man to its meaning.
rows.anchor: واللام في ولمن انتصر لام توكيد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari cites a reading after what they did wrong to stress that the retaliating person has no cause for blame or reproach, strongly affirming permission to vindicate himself.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: ويفسره قراءة من قرأ: بعد ما ظلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blameworthy path belongs to those who oppress, act arrogantly, and spread corruption; another explanation specifies killing, taking property, and bodily or verbal harm.
rows.anchor: أي سبيل الإثم والحرج، على الذين يظلمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aggression is singled out from other forms of wrongdoing to emphasize its gravity and the evil condition of its perpetrator.
rows.anchor: والبغي بغير الحق، فهو نوع من أنواع الظلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patience and forgiveness mean bearing injury without taking retaliation; the lām and man have several possible syntactic parses.
rows.anchor: أي على الظلم والأذى، وغفر، ولم ينتصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects al-Hawfi's proposal to omit the fa from the conditional result after inna; Sibawayh allows that omission only in poetry.
rows.anchor: لأن حذف الفاء مخصوص بالشعر عند سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative refers to the act of patiently forgiving; the phrase means that this is among matters requiring resolve, without needing an omitted pronoun if it refers to the subject.
rows.anchor: والإشارة بذلك إلى ما يفهم من مصدر صبر وغفر والعائد على الموصول المبتدأ من الخبر محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After mentioning ingratitude, God emphasizes His sovereignty over the upper and lower worlds and His power to give daughters, sons, both, or barrenness according to His will.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر أنه يكفر النعم، أتبع ذلك بأن له ملك العالم

rows.speaker: إسحاق بن بشر
rows.claim: Ishaq ibn Bishr says the verse was revealed concerning prophets and then generalized: Lut had daughters, Abraham sons, Muhammad both, and Yahya no children; the author adds Shuʿayb and Jesus to the examples.
rows.anchor: إسحاق بن بشر: نزلت هذه الآية في الأنبياء، ثم عمت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Daughters are mentioned first to comfort and honor them, prompting care for their protection and good treatment.
rows.anchor: وقدم تعالى هبة البنات تأنيسا لهن وتشريفا لهن

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A hadith says that whoever is tried with daughters and treats them well will find them a shield from the Fire.
rows.anchor: من ابتلي بشيء من هذه البنات فأحسن إليهن كن له سترا من النار

rows.speaker: واثلة بن الأسقع
rows.claim: Wathila ibn al-Asqaʿ calls a woman fortunate when she has a daughter before a son, since God began with daughters.
rows.anchor: واثلة بن الأسقع: من يمن المرأة تبكيرها بالأنثى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains the order by the preceding mention of trial: Arabs treated daughters as a trial, so sons are mentioned later but marked as definite to compensate for the delay and signal distinction.
rows.anchor: لأنه ذكر البلاء في آخر الآية الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations for listing females before males are to move from grief to joy, teach acceptance of God's choice, show that a son is an added favor, or emphasize care for the more needy.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بدأ بالأنثى ثم ثنى بالذكر، لتنقله من الغم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the pairing means that a woman first bears a boy and then a girl.
rows.anchor: مجاهد: هو أن تلد المرأة غلاما

rows.speaker: محمد بن الحنفية
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya says the pairing means twins, a boy and a girl.
rows.anchor: محمد بن الحنفية: أن تلد توأما، غلاما

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن العربي
rows.claim: Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi adds that God may pair people by marrying them to both sexes; scholars explain this through Adam and Eve's alternating male-female twins marrying across births.
rows.anchor: أبو بكر بن العربي: أو يزوجهم ذكرانا وإناثا. قال علماؤنا: يعني آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revelation may be inspiration cast into the heart or a dream, as with Moses' mother and Abraham; Mujahid says the Psalms were revealed to David in his heart, and a verse by ʿUbayd ibn al-Abras illustrates inspiration.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد: أوحى الله الزبور إلى داود

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: A second mode is hearing God's created speech from behind a veil without seeing the speaker, as in God's speaking with Moses and the angels.
rows.anchor: وإما على أن يسمعه كلامه الذي يخلقه في بعض الأجرام من غير أن يبصر السامع

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: A third mode is God sending an angel messenger to convey revelation, as with prophets other than Moses.
rows.anchor: وإما على أن يرسل إليه رسولا من الملائكة فيوحي الملك إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author identifies al-Zamakhshari's account as Muʿtazili because it denies that God can be seen and denies real divine speech.
rows.anchor: وهو على طريق المعتزلة في استحالة رؤية الله تعالى ونفي الكلام الحقيقي عن الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All three modes count as revelation, but the first is specially named wahi here because inspiration enters the heart all at once.
rows.anchor: وكل هذه الأقسام الثلاثة يصدق عليها أنها وحي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the first as revelation through angels and the last as a human prophet sent to address a community; it leaves out the behind-the-veil mode.
rows.anchor: وقيل: وحيا كما أوحى إلى الرسل بواسطة الملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers have singular hijab, while Ibn Abi ʿAbla reads the plural hujub.
rows.anchor: الجمهور: حجاب، مفردا وابن أبي عبلة: حجب جمعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers put yursila in the subjunctive and connect it to an omitted verb meaning He speaks from behind a veil; attaching it directly to God speaking would corrupt the meaning.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز أن يطف أو يرسل على أن يكلمه الله لفساد المعنى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats wahi and an yursila as verbal nouns functioning as circumstantial expressions, with behind a veil also expressing circumstance.
rows.anchor: وأن يرسل، مصدران واقعان موقع الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says verbal nouns as circumstantial expressions are not generally productive, and Sibawayh explicitly forbids an plus a verb from functioning as a circumstantial phrase.
rows.anchor: ومنع سيبويه أن يقع أن والفعل المقدر بالمصدر موقع الحال

none: End-of-section notice and the next surah heading only.
Qur'an text only, including verse 45:24, with no commentary in this segment.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya says the surah is Meccan without disagreement; al-Mawardi exempts 45:14 as Medinan, revealed about ʿUmar, as reported by Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مكية، قال ابن عطية: بلا خلاف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas reports that a polytheist insulted ʿUmar in Mecca before the Hijra; ʿUmar was about to strike him when the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس: نزلت في عمر: شتمه مشرك بمكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah's opening clearly echoes the previous surah's conclusion, moving from God making the Qur'an easy in the Prophet's language to the revelation of the Book.
rows.anchor: ومناسبة أولها لآخر ما قبلها في غاية الوضوح

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi prefers al-Aziz al-Hakim as an adjective of God, which is literal and closer, rather than an adjective of the Book, which he calls figurative.
rows.anchor: يجوز جعله صفة لله، فيكون ذلك حقيقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects attaching those adjectives to the Book because min Allah separates them from it; a modifier cannot be split from its noun in this construction.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي ردد في قوله: وإن جعلناه صفة للكتاب لا يجوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Signs in heaven and earth are not limited to creation: any feature, including ordering and illumination, may be a sign; the text leaves many subtle signs for reason and revelation to disclose.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه لا يراد التخصيص بالخلق، بل في السموات والأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs are attributed to believers because faith includes reason and assent.
rows.anchor: وجعلها للمؤمنين، إذ في ضمن الإيمان العقل والتصديق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The creatures spread through the earth means species other than humans and is coordinated with the phrase about human creation.
rows.anchor: وما يبث من دابة، أي في غير جنسكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author accepts coordination to a genitive pronoun without repeating the preposition, an analysis supported by the Kufians, Yunus, al-Akhfash, and al-Shalubin; al-Zamakhshari calls it poor.
rows.anchor: ومن أجاز العطف على الضمير المخفوض من غير إعادة الخافض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who are certain are people whose reflection leads them to certainty; discussion of night and day follows an earlier treatment in al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: وهم الذين لهم نظر يؤديهم إلى اليقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings vary among plural and singular ayat, nominative and accusative; the author discusses whether the construction coordinates complements governed by different factors and rejects treating waw itself as a governor.
rows.anchor: فاستدل به وشبهه مما جاء في كلام الأخفش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading explicitly repeats fi before alternation, supporting an understood preposition in other readings; further variants have alternation or wind-sending as singular or plural signs.
rows.anchor: أن في مقدرة قراءة عبد الله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari describes a progression: observing heaven and earth establishes a Creator, reflection on people and animals deepens certainty, and recurring natural changes complete knowledge through reason.
rows.anchor: إذا نظروا في السموات والأرض النظر الصحيح

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi says this passage gives six signs rather than al-Baqara's eight, omitting ships and clouds because wind governs their motion; here the signs form three groups.
rows.anchor: ذكر في البقرة ثمانية دلائل، وهنا ستة

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi reads the three conclusions as a descending appeal: believers should understand, and those without faith or certainty should at least use reason; he also distinguishes creation from created things.
rows.anchor: فلا أقل أن تكونوا من العاقلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs are the previously listed proofs, recited with truth and presented as a circumstantial phrase; the author disputes al-Zamakhshari's proposed governor for the circumstance.
rows.anchor: تلك آيات الله: أي تلك الآيات

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya says netluha may omit a noun, meaning We recite their subject and explain their lesson; alternatively the signs are the Qur'an itself, with no omission.
rows.anchor: ابن عطية: نتلوها، فيه حذف مضاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Netluha means God commands the angel to recite, and the recited truth is established by rational proofs; another reading has third-person yatluha referring to God.
rows.anchor: ونتلوها معناه: يأمر الملك أن نتلوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question what message people will believe after God's speech is a reproach, rebuke, and threat; after God means after His Book and speech, with al-Dahhak offering after God's oneness.
rows.anchor: فبأي حديث الآية، فيه تقريع وتوبيخ وتهديد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes after God and His signs to mean after God's signs by ellipsis; the author rejects this as an improper grammatical conversion of coordination into apposition.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: بعد الله وآياته، أي بعد آيات الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says a coordinated noun and its possessive each remain independently admired; construing them as one appositional phrase distorts the syntax.
rows.anchor: أن ذات زيد أعجبته، وأعجبه كرمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers differ between third-person yuʾminun and second-person tuʾminun; Talha has a variant taqninun meaning you become certain.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر، والأعرج، وشيبة، وقتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning is said to concern Abu Jahl or al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who bought foreign stories to distract people from listening to the Qur'an; it applies generally to anyone harming God's religion.
rows.anchor: قيل: نزلت في أبي جهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Afaak and athim are intensive forms, and the wording was discussed earlier.
rows.anchor: والآية عامة فيمن كان مضارا لدين الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant reads ʿulima passively, meaning the verses became known to him.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: علم وقتادة ومطر الوراق

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says thumma marks how astonishing it is that someone persists arrogantly after hearing and seeing God's clear proofs, as in a poetic example about seeing and then entering death's dangers.
rows.anchor: فمعنى ثم: الإيذان بأن فعل المقدم عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The feminine plural pronoun in اتخذها suggests that a person who recognizes one item as revelation proceeds to mock all the verses, not only the particular one heard.
rows.anchor: اتخذها هزوا، ولم يقل: اتخذه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says a stubborn person may seize an ambiguous phrase as a pretext to attack all revelation, as Ibn al-Zibʿara did with 21:98 when arguing with the Prophet.
rows.anchor: افتراص ابن الزبعرى قوله عز وجل: إنكم وما تعبدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative أولئك first follows kull in the singular, then takes plural agreement by meaning, just as in 2:53.
rows.anchor: حمل أولا على لفظ كل، وأفرد على المعنى فجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell is before them; their earnings and the idols they adopted cannot benefit them, while the Qur'an is guidance in the fullest sense.
rows.anchor: من ورائهم جهنم: أي من قدامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading has alīm nominative as an adjective of punishment, while the other reading has it genitive as an adjective of rijz.
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة، وابن محيصن، وأهل مكة، وابن كثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sea and ships show God's power: He made the vast sea serve fragile human vessels, and His command means His power, figuratively as if He ordered ships to sail.
rows.anchor: آية اعتبار في تسخير هذا المخلوق العظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's bounty includes trade, diving for pearls and coral, and obtaining fresh meat.
rows.anchor: من فضله بالتجارة وبالغوص على اللؤلؤ والمرجان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavenly things include sun, moon, stars, clouds, winds, air, and angels appointed over them; earthly things include livestock, water, mountains, and plants.
rows.anchor: ما في السماوات من الشمس والقمر والنجوم والسحاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read minhu; a variant attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas is disputed by Abu Hatim but reported by several authorities, and Salama ibn Muharib has further case and vowel variants.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: منه، وابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the common reading all these things originate with God, who creates them by power and wisdom and then subjects them to people; al-Zamakhshari offers alternate parses the author says require al-Akhfash's grammar.
rows.anchor: على قراءة الجمهور: أنه سخر هذه الأشياء

rows.speaker: السدي ومحمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Al-Suddi and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb say the command came early in Islam, telling believers to overlook the polytheists' wrongs and patiently refrain from punishing them; some call it abrogated by the sword verse, while others say it remains in force.
rows.anchor: أمر المؤمنين أن يتجاوزوا عن الكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's days means His blows against enemies and vengeance; Mujahid also explains it as days of favor, victory, and Paradise, or appointed times of promised reward.
rows.anchor: لا يرجون أيام الله: أي وقائعه بأعدائه ونقمته منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is said to have preceded fighting and its ruling to have been abrogated; Ibn ʿAbbas's report identifies its occasion as an insult to ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: قيل: نزلت قبل آية القتال ثم نسخ حكمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings of li-yajzi include the majority's third-person form, a first-person plural variant, and passive forms; the passive reading supports making a prepositional phrase the agent-like subject while retaining a direct object.
rows.anchor: وقد روي ذلك عن عاصم، وفيه حجة لمن أجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive li-yujza reading is analyzed as promoting the prepositional phrase while retaining qawman as direct object, an analysis most grammarians reject; another parse treats al-jazāʾ as the passive verb's cognate noun with an omitted verb supplying the sense.
rows.anchor: ولا يجيز ذلك الجمهور. وخرجت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author identifies the people rewarded as the forgiving believers, describing them honorifically; another view identifies them as those who do not expect God's days and will be repaid for their sins.
rows.anchor: وقوما هنا يعني به الغافرين، ونكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Good action benefits its doer and evil harms its doer; the lām marks the advantage or adversity in a figurative idiom of elevation and dominance.
rows.anchor: من عمل صالحا كهؤلاء الغافرين، ومن أساء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Judgment means adjudication and deciding matters because Israel had kingship; another view reads hukm as jurisprudence.
rows.anchor: وفصل الأمور لأن الملك كان فيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel received lawful delights, including manna and quails and the good provisions of blessed Syria, completing their favor.
rows.anchor: من الطيبات المستلذات الحلال، وبذلك تتم النعمة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Clear proofs mean evidence from revelation that settles matters; Ibn ʿAbbas says the matter foretold the Prophet's migration from Tihama to Yathrib, while another view refers to Moses' miracles.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: من الأمر، أي من أمر النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel's dispute after knowledge arose from envy among themselves; the author notes that this was explained earlier in Surah al-Shura.
rows.anchor: فما اختلفوا إلا من بعد ما جاءهم العلم بغيا بينهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After recounting Israel's blessings and later disagreement, God addresses the Prophet's special favor by placing him on a divinely prescribed law and commanding him to follow it.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر تعالى إنعامه على بني إسرائيل واختلافهم بعد ذلك

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada defines the law as commands, prohibitions, limits, and obligations.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: الشريعة: الأمر

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says the law is clear proof because it provides a path to truth.
rows.anchor: مقاتل: البينة، لأنها طريق إلى الحق

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says it is the prophetic way modeled on earlier prophets.
rows.anchor: الكلبي: السنة، لأنه كان يستن بطريقة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd defines the law as religion, which is a path to salvation.
rows.anchor: ابن زيد: الدين، لأنه طريق إلى النجاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic, shariʿa is a watering place by rivers; religious law is named by analogy as the place people draw from God's command, mercy, and nearness.
rows.anchor: والشريعة في كلام العرب: الموضع الذي يرد فيه الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ignorant whose whims must not be followed are said to be the Jews of Qurayza and Nadir or Quraysh leaders who urged the Prophet to return to his forefathers' faith.
rows.anchor: قيل: جهال قريظة والنضير. وقيل:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an is insight into religious landmarks for hearts, like spirit and life; a variant reads hādhī, referring to these verses.
rows.anchor: أي هذا القرآن جعل ما نافية من معالم الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Am hasiba is a disconnected am understood as bal plus an interrogative, making the question a denial.
rows.anchor: أم منقطعة تتقدر ببل والهمزة

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the verse concerns Ali, Hamza, and ʿUbayda against ʿUtba, Shayba, and al-Walid ibn ʿUtba, who claimed their worldly advantage would mean a better afterlife.
rows.anchor: الكلبي: نزلت في علي، وحمزة، وعبيدة بن الحرث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iqtaraḥū means they earned, the sins here are disbelief, and alladhīna supplies the second object needed to complete the sense of make them like the believers.
rows.anchor: واجترحوا: اكتسبوا، والسيئات: هنا سيئات الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about their life and death may refer only to the wrongdoers, saying their two conditions are alike, or to wrongdoers and believers, implying equal humiliation and lack of honor for both.
rows.anchor: واحتمل الضمير في محياهم ومماتهم أن يعود على الذين اجترحوا

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: Abu al-Darda says people will be resurrected in the state in which they died; Mujahid specifies that believers die and rise as believers and disbelievers as disbelievers.
rows.anchor: أبو الدرداء: يبعث الناس على ما ماتوا عليه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya says the phrase about life and death might attach to the preceding clause about bad deeds, though he considers the earlier analysis better; the author asks how this attachment works.
rows.anchor: ابن عطية: مقتضى هذا الكلام أنه لفظ الآية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats the sentence about life and death as a substitute for the pronoun in like them, since a clause can occupy the position of a second object.
rows.anchor: الزمخشري: والجملة التي هي: سواء محياهم ومماتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the proposed substitution and the parsing after make as an equalizing transformation; if attached to the prior clause, the sentence is circumstantial: they are not alike while living and dying.
rows.anchor: وتلك الجملة الواقعة بعد مفعول صيرت المقدرة مفعولا ثانيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings vary between nominative and accusative sawāʾ, with alternate parses for the case of the following words; al-Aʿmash reads both maḥyāhum and mamātuhum accusative as temporal expressions.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش: سواء بالنصب، محياهم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari also treats life and death as times, but the author rejects his analogy to the setting of a star because khufuq is only a verbal noun while maḥyā and mamāt are inherently also time and place nouns.
rows.anchor: إنكار أن يستوي المسيئون والمحسنون محيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author corrects Ibn ʿAtiyya's report of readings and says al-Tahrir repeats that transcription error; the actual readings should be taken as he has just listed them.
rows.anchor: وقد خلط ابن عطية في نقل القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse also exposes the difference between a sinful believer and an obedient believer and became a cause of devotional weeping.
rows.anchor: ويستنبط من هذه الآية تباين حال المؤمن العاصي من حال الطائع

rows.speaker: تميم الداري
rows.claim: Tamim al-Dari wept and repeated the verse through the night while praying at the Maqam.
rows.anchor: تميم الداري، رضي الله عنه، أنه كان يصلي ذات ليلة

rows.speaker: الربيع بن خيثم
rows.claim: Al-Rabiʿ ibn Khuthaym is also said to have repeated it for an entire night.
rows.anchor: الربيع بن خيثم، أنه كان يرددها ليلة أجمع

rows.speaker: الفضيل بن عياض
rows.claim: Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad used the verse to ask himself which of the two groups he belonged to.
rows.anchor: الفضيل بن عياض، كان يقول لنفسه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya says the wording suggests sins of disbelief because disbelief is contrasted with faith, but it could contrast deeds while both groups share faith, which explains the fearful readers' tears.
rows.anchor: ابن عطية: وأما لفظها فيعطي أنه اجتراح الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sāʾa mā yaḥkumūn parallels biʾsa mā ishtaraw, whose syntax was explained in al-Baqara; Ibn ʿAtiyya takes mā as a verbal noun, meaning their judgment is bad.
rows.anchor: بئسما اشتروا ، وتقدم إعرابه في البقرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation in truth means creation for a just purpose and the outpouring of benefits, and it points to the Creator as workmanship points to its maker.
rows.anchor: بالحق: بأن خلقها حق، واجب لما فيه من فيض الخيرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in litujzā may be purposive and coordinated with bil-haqq; al-Zamakhshari alternatively supplies an omitted purpose of demonstrating divine power, and Ibn ʿAtiyya reads it as a consequence.
rows.anchor: ولتجزى: هي لام كي معطوفة على بالحق

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says the question about taking one's desire as a god was revealed about al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi; afarāʾayta means tell me, with an omitted second object inferred from who can guide him afterward.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: نزلت في الحرث بن قيس السهمي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking desire as one's god means obeying every impulse as if worshipping it; Ibn Jubayr identifies the idols, while Qatada says the person does whatever he desires without fearing God.
rows.anchor: من اتخذ إلهه هواه: أي هو مطواع لهوى نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings include feminine ilāhatan and plural ālihatan, with Ibn Khalawayh explaining the plural as switching worship from one desired stone to another.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعرج، وأبو جعفر: إلهة، بتاء التأنيث

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says every Qur'anic mention of desire condemns it; Wahb advises choosing the option farther from one's desire, and Sahl al-Tustari calls desire a disease cured by resisting it.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: ما ذكر الله هوى إلا ذمه

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A hadith calls incapable the person who follows his own desire and merely indulges hopes about God.
rows.anchor: العاجز من أتبع نفسه هواها وتمنى على الله الأماني

rows.speaker: عنترة
rows.claim: The pre-Islamic poet ʿAntara presents himself as generous and noble, refusing to follow his stubborn soul's desire; the line witnesses the word hawā.
rows.anchor: قول عنترة، وهو جاهلي: إني امرؤ وسمح الخليقة ماجد

rows.speaker: أبو عمران موسى بن عمران الإشبيلي
rows.claim: The ascetic Abu ʿImran urges resisting desire, warning that obeying it leads to the worst paths and a disastrous fall; his lines use hawā as the governing impulse.
rows.anchor: أبو عمران موسى بن عمران الإشبيلي الزاهد، رحمه الله تعالى: فخالف هواها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God led him astray upon knowledge can mean God's prior knowledge or the person's knowing truth while rejecting it in defiance, as in 27:14.
rows.anchor: على علم من هذا الضال بأن الحق هو الدين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains the leading astray as withholding guidance and favor with knowledge that it would not benefit the person; the author identifies this as Muʿtazili theology.
rows.anchor: وهو على طريقة الاعتزال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings of ghishāwa differ in vowel and form across readers and dialects; ta-dhakkarun is geminated for most, light for al-Jahdari, and has two tāʾs for al-Aʿmash.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: تذكرون، بشد الذال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial that there is only worldly life is attributed to some Quraysh rejecting resurrection.
rows.anchor: حياتنا الدنيا : هي مقالة بعض قريش إنكارا للبعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning of we die and live describes humanity collectively, one group dying and another living; another view reverses the sequence, and others take it to mean nonexistence followed by existence or parents followed by children.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قولهم: نموت ونحيا حكم على النوع بجملته

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAli reads wa-naḥyā with a damma on the initial nūn.
rows.anchor: زيد بن علي: ونحيا، بضم النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dahr means the length of time in which calamities accumulate; if the speakers believe in God they wrongly attribute events to time, and if they deny God they are materialist Dahriyya attributing them to time.
rows.anchor: وما يهلكنا إلا الدهر: أي طول الزمان

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abdullah reads illa dahr, with an omitted verb understood as time passing; Arabs attributed every event to time and complained about it in poetry.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله: إلا دهر، وتأويله:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One analysis makes the day of the Hour depend on خسِر and treats yawmئذ as a substitute, but the author says the compensating tanwin already points to the same day, making an ordinary substitute redundant.
rows.anchor: العامل في ويوم تقوم: يخسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another group supplies an omitted reference to God's sovereignty on Judgment Day, since the transformed Day is neither heaven nor earth; yawmئذ itself is governed by يخسر.
rows.anchor: العامل: في ويوم تقوم ما يدل عليه الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mubtilun means those who entered into falsehood; jāthiya is kneeling and poised in the posture of a guilty, fearful person.
rows.anchor: جاثية: باركة على الركب مستوفزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variant jādhiya with dhāl describes an even more poised posture, sitting on the tips of the toes; Ibn ʿAbbas says gathered, Qatada says groups, Murajj says submissive, and ʿIkrima says distinguished.
rows.anchor: جاذية، بالذال والجذو أشد استيفازا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says each nation is called at the time of accounting; Yahya ibn Sallam restricts this to disbelievers summoned to the scripture or record by which they are judged.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: وذلك عند الحساب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations of their book include the record written by the angels, the Preserved Tablet, or what has been decreed for them; the singular uses a generic collective noun.
rows.anchor: أو الذي كتبته الحفظة، وهو صحائف أعمالها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The book is attributed both to God as owner and commander of its writing and to each nation because its deeds are recorded in it; minimal association suffices for either attribution.
rows.anchor: وصحت إضافته إليه تعالى لأنه مالكه والآمر بكتبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their bad deeds means either the ugliness of their acts or the punishments for them; punishment is called a bad deed by analogy, as in 42:40.
rows.anchor: وبدا لهم سيئات ما عملوا: أي قبائح أعمالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb ḥāqa means to surround and is used only for something unpleasant.
rows.anchor: وحاق بهم أي أحاط، ولا يستعمل حاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: We forget you means either leave you in punishment or treat you like a discarded, forgotten thing; forgetting the meeting of the day means failing to expect God's recompense despite warnings.
rows.anchor: ننساكم: نترككم في العذاب، أو نجعلكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase meeting of the day is an expansive genitive construction like the Qur'anic phrase scheming of night and day in 34:33.
rows.anchor: وأضاف اللقاء لليوم توسعا كقوله: بل مكر الليل والنهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read lā yukhrajūn passively, while al-Hasan, Ibn Waththab, Hamza, and al-Kisaʾi read it actively; min-hā means from the Fire.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: لا يخرجون، مبنيا للمفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They are not granted a chance to make amends by returning to righteous action; the discussion of istʿitāb was given earlier.
rows.anchor: ولا هم يستعتبون أي بطلب مراجعة إلى عمل صالح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers put rabb in the genitive in all three occurrences as an adjective; Ibn Muhaysin reads two in the nominative with an implied huwa.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: رب، بالجر في الثلاثة على الصفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ahqaf is a long, raised sand dune with a bend; the verb ihqawqafa means to become crooked, as witnessed by Imruʾ al-Qays's line.
rows.anchor: الحقف: رمل مستطيل مرتفع فيه اعوجاج وانحناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ʿaniya describes being perplexed about a matter when its direction is unknown; it may assimilate to ʿayya, as illustrated by a poetic line about a dove confused over its egg.
rows.anchor: عنى بالأمر: إذا لم تعرف جهته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada say the passage about the revelation being from God and the command to be patient are Medinan, while the rest of the surah is Meccan.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس وقتادة، أن: قل أرأيتم إن كان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The new surah answers the previous ending's charge that the Prophet mocked God's signs and fabricated revelation; the same divine attributes close one surah and open the next.
rows.anchor: ومناسبة أولها لما قبلها، أن في آخر ما قبلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An appointed term means the time when this bodily structure will decay; Ibn ʿAbbas identifies it as the Resurrection, while another view takes it as each creature's lifespan.
rows.anchor: وأجل مسمى: أي موعد لفساد هذه البنية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ʿammā unḏirū, mā may be a verbal noun or a relative pronoun.
rows.anchor: عما أنذروا: يحتمل أن تكون ما مصدرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idols people call on are challenged to identify anything they created on earth; the question rebukes them, and the interrogative is the second object of areaytum while also suspending arūnī.
rows.anchor: قل أرأيتم ما تدعون: معناه أخبروني عن الذين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arūnī may instead emphasize areaytum in the sense of tell me, with its second object omitted.
rows.anchor: ويمكن أن يكون أروني توكيدا لأرأيتم
